title: Mapping open quantum dynamics onto graphs
authors: Kyuho Kim, Dayeong Lee, Seungkyun Park, Xianji Piao, Namkyoo Park, Sunkyu Yu
abstract: Graph-theoretic frameworks have been widely employed in quantum physics to address the high-dimensional complexity of quantum systems. Although open quantum dynamics incorporates system-bath coupling via numerous interacting operators, it has been formulated algebraically with a partial set of jump operators or statistically universal reservoirs, leaving the underlying connectivity structure largely unexplored. Here, we propose a universal graph-theoretic framework for Markovian quantum dynamics. The framework maps open quantum dynamics onto two uniquely defined graphs, where the quantum master equation is rigorously interpreted as the average wave characteristic of operator-valued signals across the graphs. Applying this framework to the open quantum Rabi model, we demonstrate an open-system generalization of Fock-state lattices, characterize graph-topological signatures of dissipation, and classify the weak-to-ultrastrong coupling transition. Building on these representations, graph pruning reveals the backbone of open quantum dynamics, which enables superior graph neural-network learning. Our results bridge graph theory and open quantum dynamics, achieving efficient data-driven analysis of high-dimensional complexity.
summary: The paper introduces a universal graph-theoretic framework to analyze open quantum dynamics by mapping the system's evolution onto two distinct graphs. By applying this to the Open Quantum Rabi Model, the authors demonstrate that graph structures can characterize dissipation and coupling regimes. They further show that Graph Neural Networks trained on these pruned graphs can accurately predict the complex Liouville spectrum.
main_problem: To develop a universal graph-theoretic framework for mapping and analyzing open quantum dynamics, addressing the unexplored connectivity structure of system-bath coupling.
main_result: The authors propose a framework that maps Markovian open quantum dynamics onto two uniquely defined graphs ($G_H$ and $G_L$), allowing for efficient data-driven analysis using graph neural networks (GNNs). Graph pruning was shown to preserve spectral features significantly better than direct matrix sparsification.
method: The method involves representing the Lindblad master equation evolution via operator-valued signals on magnetic graphs, followed by applying graph pruning and training a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to predict the Liouville spectrum.
model_or_system: The study focuses on open quantum systems undergoing Markovian dynamics, exemplified by the Open Quantum Rabi Model (QRM). The evolution is governed by the Lindblad Master Equation involving system-bath coupling terms ($\kappa, \gamma, \gamma_\phi$).
key_observables: Liouville spectrum (eigenvalues $\lambda$), graph topologies ($G_H, G_L$), and spectral diagnostics like the Chamfer distance $D$ used to quantify approximation accuracy.
important_parameters: Coupling strengths ($\kappa, \gamma, \gamma_\phi$), pruning threshold ($\chi$), and coupling regimes such as weak-to-ultrastrong coupling (USC).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the dynamics can be accurately characterized by two graph structures ($G_H$ and $G_L$) derived from the Lindblad form, and that a GCN trained on these graphs can predict the spectrum.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QRM graphs ($G_H, G_L$), show spectral differences across dissipation regimes, compare graph pruning vs. matrix sparsification using Chamfer distance, and demonstrate optimal GCN performance at specific pruning thresholds ($\chi$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the universal graph framework for open dynamics, applies it to the QRM model, details the use of graph measures and spectral analysis, compares graph pruning against standard matrix methods, and finally demonstrates predictive power using a trained Graph Convolutional Network.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful mathematical bridge between advanced concepts in quantum optics (open systems) and modern machine learning tools (GNNs), offering new diagnostic tools for understanding dissipation mechanisms in complex quantum devices.
